title: Tarun Tejpal: Tehelka founder sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape
description: An Indian court has sentenced former Tehelka magazine editor Tarun Tejpal to 10 years in prison for raping a former colleague, overturning his 2021 ac
body: An Indian court has sentenced former Tehelka magazine editor Tarun Tejpal to 10 years in prison for raping a former colleague, overturning his 2021 acquittal in a decade-old case.The Goa bench of the Bombay High Court convicted Tejpal under sections of Indian law pertaining to rape and sexual harassment.Along with jail terms which run concurrently, the court has also ordered him to pay fines adding up to more than 1mn rupees ($10,500; £7,800).Tejpal, who has denied the accusations, said before the sentencing that he would file an appeal in the Supreme Court.The allegations against Tejpal, one of India's best-known editors, had made national headlines in 2013. A year before that, thousands of Indians had participated in protests after a brutal gang rape and murder of a woman in Delhi, leading to a larger conversation on sexual violence.Tejpal's accuser, who cannot be identified under Indian law, said that he sexually assaulted her in a lift during Tehelka's high-profile international conference in Goa in November 2013, an event attended by, among others, Hollywood star Robert De Niro. Judge questions 'appropriate' behaviour for rape victimsTarun Tejpal: Powerful and pioneering journalistTejpal initially blamed the assault on "a lapse of judgement" and "a misreading of the situation" which had "led to an unfortunate incident that rails against all we believe in and fight for".But as the case escalated, he issued a statement urging authorities to examine the CCTV footage "so the accurate version of events stands clearly revealed". He also alleged that the case against him was part of a "political vendetta" by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government in Goa.Tehelka, the magazine Tejpal co-founded in 2000, had published a number of scoops, many of them based on sting operations.Some of these stories - including Operation West End in which some of its journalists posed as arms dealers, secretly filming senior army officials, bureaucrats and even the president of the then ruling BJP taking bribes to push through a fake deal - created national and international ripples.Tejpal was arrested in 2013 and spent seven months in jail until the Supreme Court granted him bail.In 2021, a sessions court in Goa threw out all the charges against him. But the judge's observations in the 527-page order sparked criticism after she questioned the behaviour of the survivor..In photographs taken shortly after the assault, the judge wrote, the young woman was "smiling and looked happy, normal, in [a] good mood"."She did not look disturbed, reserved, terrified or traumatised in any way even though this was immediately after she claims to have been sexually assaulted," the order said. The Goa government had appealed against the acquittal in the high court. Appearing for the Goa government, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta had urged the high court to impose the maximum sentence on Tejpal."This court must give a clear message to society that when a girl says no, it means no," Livelaw quoted him as saying."All I can say is I am 62. I believe I am a political victim. I am a father of two daughters. I have a wife. All we can say is we will go up and appeal. My lawyer wants me to request you to be lenient," legal website Bar and Bench quoted Tejpal as telling the court before the sentencing.Tejpal was found guilty under legal sections including 376(2)(f), which pertains to rape committed by "a relative, guardian or teacher of, or a person in a position of trust or authority towards the woman".

schema.headline: Tarun Tejpal: Tehelka founder sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape

title: David Owori: Outrage as Ugandan football captain beaten to death in street gang attack
description: Ugandans are mourning the death at 27 of one of the country's best-known footballers after he was beaten by suspected robbers near his home in the cap
body: Ugandans are mourning the death at 27 of one of the country's best-known footballers after he was beaten by suspected robbers near his home in the capital, Kampala.Police said David Owori was fatally assaulted after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings, prompting an outpouring of grief and renewed public anger over violent crime in Uganda.Owori captained Sports Club (SC) Villa, the Uganda Premier League record champions, where he played both as a right-back and midfielder. He also represented the country's national team - the Cranes."We have lost more than a player - we have lost a leader, brother and friend," SC Villa said in a statement. Witnesses said a group of attackers hit the footballer with paving stones on Tuesday night before robbing Owori of his belongings and fleeing, leaving him unconscious.SC Villa spokesperson Asan Kasingye told journalists that Owori was targeted just outside his home in Makindye, a Kampala suburb. "The player was ambushed by thugs as he approached his home, leaving him with life-threatening injuries before he was rushed to the medical facility," Kasingye said. Owori was rushed to a nearby medical clinic and then transferred to a private facility in the city, but he died of his injuries on Wednesday.Local police spokesperson Rachael Kawala said detectives were pursuing leads to identify those responsible."The scene of the incident has been documented and processed to ensure that all relevant evidence is collected and preserved," Kawala added. Owori's murder has sent shockwaves across Uganda, with the football community, including fans and teammates, and politicians demanding justice. Tributes are continuing to pour in for the defender, who was popularly known as Colgate. The Federation of Uganda Football Associations (Fufa) described Owori as "a true leader on and off the pitch"."David was not just a footballer. He was both a leader and an inspiration to a generation," it said in a statement. The national side, the Cranes, said the team had lost a football star who "carried the hopes" of Uganda. Parliament on Wednesday observed a minute's silence in honour of Owori and called for a quick investigation. The versatile player, renowned for his tactical discipline and ability to feature across midfield, returned to SC Villa in 2023 - after two years in Europe - for a second spell. At the time of his death, he was among the longest-serving members of the current squad.He helped lead the high-profile team to their first league title in 20 years securing a record 17th top-flight crown in 2024.  His influence on and off the pitch earned him a contract extension until January 2027 with the team. Owori also featured in the national team during the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign and was regarded as a strong contender for future call-ups to the Cranes.His death has triggered anger on social media, with many Ugandans questioning the level of violent crime in Kampala and calling for tougher action against criminals. The killing comes just weeks after the death of another Ugandan sports star - rugby international Sydney Gongodyo - who was also fatally attacked by a mob in Kampala

schema.headline: David Owori: Outrage as Ugandan football captain beaten to death in street gang attack

title: Rihanna working on new music, says A$AP Rocky
description: Rihanna could be set to break a decade-long album hiatus, according to her partner A$AP Rocky."She in the studio right now," the rapper said on the Th
body: Rihanna could be set to break a decade-long album hiatus, according to her partner A$AP Rocky."She in the studio right now," the rapper said on the The Jason Lee podcast on Wednesday. Few details about the project were revealed, apart from a denial that the pair would collaborate on a double album. However, in response to questioning about about a potential new album, he added "she cooking."The singer and beauty mogul from Barbados, whose real name is Robyn Fenty, has not released a full album since 2016's Anti."Are you the reason we don't have an album?" podcaster Jason Lee asked the rapper on his show, noting the three children shared by the pair and Rihanna's travel.The rapper denied this, instead saying that the singer was in fact working on new music."Yeah I said it, sorry babe," he continued, adding that he would "get in trouble for this."Little other information about the possible music was revealed in the interview.In February last year, Rihanna said that she felt "really optimistic" about a new album. "I feel like I've finally cracked it, girl!," she told a reporter from Harper's Bazaar.She also said, "I cannot put up anything mediocre. After waiting eight years, you might as well just wait some more."Since her last album, Rihanna has released singles, including some linked to film projects, including 2022's Lift Me Up for Black Panther: Wakanda Forever. She has also launched multiple businesses, including her popular makeup range Fenty Beauty and a lingerie company. The 38-year-old's net worth has been estimated by Forbes at over a billion dollars.During the interview, A$AP Rocky, real name Rakim Mayers, refused to comment on whether he and Rihanna had married.

schema.headline: Rihanna working on new music, says A$AP Rocky

title: Ex-leader Hasina gambles with vow to return to Bangladesh
description: Former Bangladeshi prime minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return to her country in December, despite facing the death penalty there for crimes agai
body: Former Bangladeshi prime minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return to her country in December, despite facing the death penalty there for crimes against humanity.Hasina, who denies the charges, was tried in absentia after fleeing to India during an anti-government uprising in 2024.On the second anniversary of being ousted, Hasina said in an audio broadcast to a crowded press club in Delhi that she "had to go back", but wouldn't announce her exact plans or dates yet.Her Awami League party has been falling apart and Indian officials have been facing pressure to extradite her after a special tribunal in Dhaka sentenced her to death last year for ordering lethal force to be used on protesters.Hasina's virtual meeting with reporters at the Foreign Correspondents' Club in Delhi was her first meeting with the media since she was toppled after 15 years in power.She delivered a speech over an audio link and then took a handful of questions. "I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she said.In the address she alleged that several organisations had turned the 2024 student protests into a "violent movement", without providing any evidence.She has always rejected the charges on which she was convicted as politically motivated. But UN investigators found evidence that she and her government tried to cling to power using systematic, deadly violence.In audio of one phone call verified by BBC Eye, Hasina was heard authorising the deadly crackdown on demonstrators. Prosecutors used the recording as crucial evidence in convicting her. The UN estimates up to 1,400 people were killed, most by gunfire from security forces, during the protests, which started as a student-led movement against quotas in government jobs and turned into a mass uprising.The 78-year-old fled Dhaka as tens of thousands of demonstrators held protests and stormed government buildings, including her official residence, plunging the country of more than 170 million into crisis.Soon after she was toppled, an interim government took charge. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party came to power after elections in February this year, with its leader Tarique Rahman now prime minister. His government had already warned local media not to publish or broadcast Hasina's comments. After her address, it said it was "outraged" India had allowed her to take part in a public meeting with the media."Our people have firmly resolved that our nation will never again go back to the dark days of fascism and that Bangladesh will never be a client state," a foreign ministry statement said. Hasina's presence in Delhi has strained relations with Bangladesh, which wants her extradited, a request India says it's examining.A return by Hasina to Dhaka, if it happens, is likely to have repercussions, including political unrest."It's a huge risk for her personally. If she does go back to Bangladesh, she will immediately be arrested," says David Bergman, an analyst based in Dhaka.It's likely that supporters of the ruling BNP, as well as the party of the students, the National Citizens Party, Islamists and others could hold rallies demanding that her sentence be carried out.But the stakes are also high for the Awami League, if she does not return.The activities of the party were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.Awami League leaders allege that hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces. Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted."If Ms Hasina doesn't go back, the violence will continue and they will exterminate the Awami League," Mohammad Ali Arafat, a former minister in Ms Hasina's cabinet, who is also overseas, told the BBC.There has been growing discontent among a section of her party that many top leaders had fled the country while leaving mid-level leaders and supporters vulnerable to attacks."It must be to do with the recognition that if Ms Hasina is going to have any relevance to Bangladesh politics in the future, she's got to go back to Bangladesh and face it," David Bergman says.

schema.headline: Ex-leader Hasina gambles with vow to return to Bangladesh

title: UN rights chief alarmed by rise in Iran executions since March
description: The UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear amon
body: The UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear among the population and suppress dissent".Volker Türk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests.More than 100 others were at risk of execution on similar charges, while executions for drug-related offences were also continuing at an alarming rate, he added.Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International.The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.Activists have warned that Iranian authorities might make greater use of executions against their opponents following January's protests, during which thousands of demonstrators were killed and tens of thousands were detained, and the US-Israeli war with Iran on 28 February.In a statement, Türk urged Iranian authorities to halt all executions and move toward the abolition of the death penalty, saying that "such punishment has no place in our world".As well as expressing alarm at the rise in executions, he said the persistent lack of fair trial and due process guarantees was "deeply troubling", with confessions allegedly obtained under torture and other ill-treatment."Several executions have reportedly been carried out in public. Some have reportedly been carried out only weeks after arrest," he added. "Twelve defendants were reportedly sentenced to death following a single three-hour closed-door hearing."There was no immediate comment from the Iranian government. But it has previously defended the use of the death penalty, saying it is limited to only "the most severe crimes".On Monday, Iran's judiciary said it executed two men convicted of spying for Israel.Omid Behzad and Pouria Safvat were accused of sending coordinates, images and other information on sensitive military, law enforcement and security sites to Israel's Mossad foreign intelligence service during the current war and the 12-day conflict in June 2025, according to the judiciary's Mizan news agency.Last week, 19-year-old Arvin Kheirkhahan was executed after being convicted of the security-related charge of "enmity against God" over his alleged role in January's unrest, Iran's Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported, citing a source close to his family.Another two men arrested during the protests, Abolfazl Sepahi Badjani and Amirhossein Safari Hosseinabadi, were executed in public in a square in Isfahan, according to HRANA.They were among 12 people convicted of several charges, including "enmity against God" and "corruption on Earth", in connection with the killing of four law enforcement officers on 8 January. Two of their fellow defendants, Erfan Esfandiari and Gol Mohammad Mohammadi, were executed on 19 July.UN human rights experts said the 12 were sentenced to death "in one hearing, in a closed courtroom and without clarity as to each defendant's individual responsibility", which violated established fair trial standards.

schema.headline: UN rights chief alarmed by rise in Iran executions since March

title: Man charged with killing Scottish aid worker in Greece
description: An Afghan boxer has been charged with killing Scottish aid worker Elisabeth Ross in Greece.Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, has been charged with homicide with in
body: An Afghan boxer has been charged with killing Scottish aid worker Elisabeth Ross in Greece.Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, has been charged with homicide with intent, alongside robbery and weapons offences.The body of Ross, who was 38, was discovered in a suitcase by a homeless man in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of the Greek capital on 18 July.Ahmadzai was remanded in custody until his trial, which could take up to 18 months. During the hearing he asked for an English translator but did not respond to the charges.Ahmadzai arrived in court in Athens on Thursday morning in an unmarked Grey car. He was escorted out with masked officers holding his head down.On Wednesday, he was assigned a court-appointed lawyer and given time to prepare his defence.Ahmadzai was initially detained on illegal weapons possession charges and is facing a charge of homicide with intent, as well as allegations that he stole more than €10,000 (£8,500) from the victim's bank accounts using her bank cards. Homicide with intent is equivalent to a murder charge in Scots law.A statement from the police's organised crime directorate said Ahmadzai was brought to a police station on 30 July. "In particular, it emerged that the 26-year-old placed the body in a suitcase and transported it to the abandoned site," the statement said.The BBC understands he denies the charge of murder but admits moving the body, claiming that he did so because he feared he would be blamed for her death.

schema.headline: Man charged with killing Scottish aid worker in Greece

title: Nigerian security forces rescue 308 abductees from Kainji Lake National Park
description: More than 300 people abducted in separate attacks in Nigeria have been rescued, the country's presidency says, in what it describes as the largest sin
body: More than 300 people abducted in separate attacks in Nigeria have been rescued, the country's presidency says, in what it describes as the largest single-day operation by joint security forces. The victims were rescued from the Kainji Lake National Park in Niger state in an operation involving the military, police, intelligence unit and the National Counter-Terrorism Centre. Those freed include 163 people abducted during a February attack on the Woro and Nuku communities in Kwara state, where scores were killed. At least 145 others had been taken in Niger state. It is not clear whether any suspects were detained in the operation.The victims were receiving medical care at a military site before being reunited with their families. "President Bola Ahmed Tinubu warmly welcomes the successful rescue of 308 Nigerian citizens who were abducted in different attacks in Niger and Kwara states," presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga said.It was "the largest rescue operation ever carried out" in a single day, Onanuga added.Tinubu described the operation as a sign of improved co-ordination among Nigeria's security agencies. The armed jihadists wanted residents of the village of Woro in Kwara State to renounce the Nigerian government and its constitution and instead follow their teachings, effectively attempting to impose a parallel system of rule and government in the area.Amnesty International said many of the dead had been found with their hands and feet tied - some had had their throats slit, others had been shot dead.The Nigerian government has blamed Boko Haram for the attack - the jihadist group has not issued any statement about it.The rescue comes weeks after 44 pupils and teachers abducted during a school attack in Oyo state were freed after more than 50 days in captivity following a month-long security operation. The series of abductions, including attacks in parts of north-central and southern Nigeria, has raised fresh concerns that insecurity is spreading beyond the country's traditional conflict zones.

schema.headline: Nigerian security forces rescue 308 abductees from Kainji Lake National Park

title: Tewolde Gebremariam: Air India's new CEO faces financial and safety turbulence
description: Air India has appointed a new chief executive as the airline grapples with mounting challenges, including heavy financial losses and the fallout from
body: Air India has appointed a new chief executive as the airline grapples with mounting challenges, including heavy financial losses and the fallout from last year's crash that killed 260 people.Tewolde Gebremariam succeeds Campbell Wilson, who stepped down from the role in April.Gebremariam was earlier CEO at Ethiopian Airlines, where he worked for over a decade, growing the regional carrier into one of Africa's largest airlines.Air India, which Tata Group bought from the Indian government in 2022, has been dealing with a period of operational turbulence.The airline operates a fleet of 198 aircraft, flying nearly 5,000 weekly flights to 91 destinations in India and abroad, according to the Air India website.Air India said Gebremariam was unanimously chosen by its board after an extensive search, citing his leadership and operational expertise to steer the airline's "next phase of growth".N Chandrasekaran, Air India chairman, said: "Having completed the initial phase of stabilisation, integration, and fleet commitments under Campbell's guidance, Air India is now entering a critical execution and expansion era."Wilson, a former Singapore Airlines executive hired after Tata Group bought Air India nearly four years ago, had signalled in 2024 that he planned to step down in 2026 and had been preparing the airline for a smooth transition.Now, his replacement Gebremariam has said that he is looking forward to building a "world-class global airline" that "reflects India's extraordinary economic potential".During his tenure at Ethiopian Airlines, Gebremariam was credited with expanding the fleet nearly threefold and growing it into Africa's most profitable airline. At Air India, however, Gebremariam faces a daunting task. He takes over as the airline grapples with a series of safety and operational challenges, led by last June's fatal Ahmedabad-London crash, a major setback to its ambitions. The final crash report is due in October.The airline has continued to struggle since returning to private ownership, reporting a record loss of nearly $2.3bn (£1.7bn) last month. Chandrasekaran has warned a turnaround could take up to a decade. The airline has also cut nearly a third of its international operations.The airline has also made headlines for a string of operational setbacks. In March, a Delhi-Vancouver flight turned back after nearly eight hours because it lacked clearance to enter Canadian airspace.These troubles come as India's wider aviation sector faces pressure from rising costs, disrupted international routes due to the Iran war, aircraft delivery delays and tighter regulatory scrutiny.Aviation experts told the BBC that Gebremariam may be the leader Air India needs, pointing to two defining crises he steered Ethiopian Airlines through: the 2019 Boeing 737 Max crash that killed 157 people and the Covid pandemic, when the airline stayed profitable by expanding its cargo business as passenger revenues collapsed."Gebremariam endeared himself to his employees during both these black swan events, especially his backing of the pilots and engineers at Ethiopian," Sanjay Lazar, CEO of Avialaz Consultants, told the BBC.At Air India, Gebremariam's priorities will include rebuilding workplace culture, lifting employee morale, accelerating delayed fleet expansion and refurbishment, and reshaping the airline's network to stem losses, experts say. Air India has not said when he will take over, saying details will be announced later.

schema.headline: Tewolde Gebremariam: Air India's new CEO faces financial and safety turbulence

title: Sonam Wangchuk: Protests weakened Narendra Modi, activist tells BBC after hunger strike
description: The recent youth-led protests have weakened Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi "terribly", says leading activist Sonam Wangchuk whose hunger strike g
body: The recent youth-led protests have weakened Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi "terribly", says leading activist Sonam Wangchuk whose hunger strike galvanised the movement.Wangchuk told the BBC that the atmosphere in the country had changed following  mass demonstrations which triggered the resignation of the education minister on 25 July.Young people now have more confidence they can "change things if they want to" and feel they don't have to "take everything lying down", the 59-year-old said.The "cockroach" movement mounted one of the biggest public displays of dissent against Modi's government, which has been in power since 2014.The movement takes its name from a remark by India's chief justice, who drew criticism after comparing sections of unemployed young people to "cockroaches" during a court hearing.Wangchuk fasted in scorching heat in the capital, Delhi, for 26 days in June and July, consuming only salt and water. He says he has now regained six of the 11kg he lost. The activist was forcibly taken to hospitals which he says were "more like prisons" for the final six days of his fast.By then, the protests had escalated from public anger about the leak of exam papers into some of the biggest anti-government demonstrations India had seen in years.Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned the day after Wangchuk ended his hunger strike.Since then, Modi has announced fast-track courts to try those accused in the leaks and appointed a tech billionaire to lead efforts to reform the examination system.The government also said it would offer compensation to families of students who took their own lives after exam questions were leaked.But India's problems are deeper - with graduate unemployment hovering around 35-40% for the past 25 years.Wangchuk argues fundamental reform to education is needed.The engineer and education specialist says exams currently have little relevance to the job market.Often based on multiple-choice questions, they are designed to assess millions of students efficiently, with no consideration of how effectively they measure skills and understanding, he says. This, in turn, shapes how schools teach.If exams placed greater emphasis on hands-on experience and aptitude, he suggests, schools might adapt their methods and help address India's jobs crisis."There needs to be some planning of what the world and the country are likely to look like in 15 years," Wangchuk says.Changing the way children are taught might help ensure they are "not left unemployed and sectors that need people are not left underemployed". India's government has previously defended itself against criticism of its handling of the economy. It argues that claims of an unemployment crisis are overstated and that its macroeconomic policy remains fundamentally robust.Wangchuk insists change is in the air in India.He believes the government has been hugely damaged by how long it took before Pradhan stepped down."This gave young people a chance to gain confidence and unity in their actions."Wangchuk says that, if the government doesn't listen to the people, they may return to protests that go beyond education.He suggests the damage is already being felt by the governing BJP, pointing to the party losing two of three by-elections this week - including a seat in Bihar state it had held for more than 30 years.However, he maintains that India's leaders could still change their approach."I always believe in people realising their mistakes and amending their ways. So I would give them that chance."Twelve days have now passed since Wangchuk said he broke his fast. He is back in Leh, his hometown in the Himalayan region of Ladakh.He has a renewed faith in the power of hunger strikes - taking inspiration from Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy of non-violent resistance.In previous years he's held hunger strikes for more self-rule in Ladakh and against a "very powerful government" seeking to "bulldoze ecologically sensitive places".Though he has not achieved his goals there, he says "inflicting pain on ourselves makes the government feel differently, compared to us using sticks and stones". Asked if he has any plans to run for office, he says no - he would rather enable others to do so.

schema.headline: Sonam Wangchuk: Protests weakened Narendra Modi, activist tells BBC after hunger strike

title: How AI is changing jobs in the Philippines' outsourcing industry
description: 'I feel like I dug my own grave': The workers caught in the AI transitionImage source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, The Philippines is kno
body: 'I feel like I dug my own grave': The workers caught in the AI transitionImage source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, The Philippines is known as the call centre capital of the worldBySuranjana TewariAsia Business CorrespondentReporting fromManilaFor 15 years, single mother Lisa made a living from content writing.She began writing straight out of college, freelanced for years and eventually followed a path taken by many young Filipinos: joining a multinational in the country's booming outsourcing industry.Lisa says she never felt the need to use artificial intelligence (AI) in her work."I can say that I am able to do my job, I meet deadlines. In my opinion, there is no need for [AI]," she told the BBC. Eight months into her latest role, and one month before the position was due to become permanent, she was made redundant.In the months before, Lisa says a public relations agency had been tasked with producing AI-generated material that she and her colleagues were asked to edit. She says her skills were used to train the AI on the company writing style."I feel like I dug my own grave," she says. "We were the ones who trained the artificial intelligence that replaced us."Lisa, not her real name, is one of several former outsourcing employees the BBC spoke to who asked to remain anonymous. They signed confidentiality agreements in return for severance pay, and fear that speaking publicly could hurt their chances of finding work in an industry which has a small network.Their experiences offer an insight into a question confronting emerging economies like the Philippines: what happens when AI begins to automate the jobs that helped lift millions of people into the middle classes?Building an industryEvery evening around 5pm, streams of workers wearing company lanyards spill out of high-rise offices in the district of Cubao in Manila.It's one of several areas of the capital where multinational companies have premises – providing all sorts of outsourcing work including call centres, accounting, software development and marketing copy services for clients thousands of miles away.For over two decades, these business districts have symbolised one of the Philippines' biggest economic success stories.Beginning in the early 2000s, the country was promoted as an English-speaking alternative to India for what's called business process outsourcing (BPO).Successive governments offered tax incentives, invested in infrastructure and encouraged multinational companies to set up large operations.Global groups like Accenture, Concentrix and Teleperformance built sprawling campuses, employing hundreds of thousands of Filipinos.Today, the outsourcing industry employs roughly 1.9 million people, and generates $40bn (£30.1bn) in revenues every year, accounting for about 10% of the Philippines' economy.But experts say the industry is disproportionately vulnerable to the impact of AI.Image caption, The outsourcing industry employs about 1.9 million people in the PhilippinesThe International Labour Organization estimates that 12.7 million Filipinos - more than one in four workers - are employed in occupations exposed to generative AI, the highest share in South East Asia.The organisation expects many roles to change rather than disappear but the types of service jobs that people do in the Philippines leaves it particularly at risk.Jack Madrid, president of the IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines (IBPAP), admits that AI is being adopted by the sector. More than two-thirds of IBPAP's members are already running AI pilots, he says."Agentic AI has the potential to automate at a much more accelerated pace," Madrid says. "Obviously, there's a layer of jobs that are automatable or have been automated."But he adds that the vast majority of affected workers have been redeployed within the same organisations.Madrid says any weakness in hiring reflects more than the impact of AI."We've seen a slowdown in investment decisions on whether certain job functions or processes should be offshored," he says, pointing to slower global demand and uncertainty over how companies will ultimately deploy the technology.Even so, he acknowledges the challenge. "We cannot do enough to be prepared," he says. "The importance of reskilling" cannot be overstated.The pressure to automateMary, another former content writer whose name we've changed, says her employer encouraged the use of AI as a productivity tool.Instead of making her job easier, she says it created additional responsibilities."We had to edit more, fact-check more because the data AI produced was inaccurate," she says. "Technically it was more work for us."Like Lisa, she was later made redundant.Companies are under pressure to implement AI, to reduce costs and increase productivity, experts say. Teleperformance, the world's largest call centre operator and one of the Philippines' biggest private employers, has said AI offers an opportunity to augment rather than replace its workforce.The company expects AI to handle routine interactions while human agents move into more complex roles. Teleperformance has also said it plans to retrain employees.Accenture has similarly said that generative AI will reshape almost every job rather than eliminate positions.The firm has promised to invest billions of dollars in AI capabilities and workforce training.Concentrix - which is the biggest outsourcing firm in the Philippines - says its AI systems should remain under human oversight and has committed to training employees in the new technology.Some Filipino managers are uneasy about AI and want to slow down adoption, according to Paul Quintos, from the University of the Philippines-Diliman. They are concerned about how much of the domestic workforce might be displaced."But there's tremendous pressure from foreign clients to adopt AI," he says. "It's a major cost-cutting measure."Philippine outsourcing companies compete directly with rivals in India and elsewhere for contracts from multinational corporations.Increasingly, those clients expect suppliers not only to provide cheaper labour, but also to integrate AI into the services they deliver.Image caption, The BBC spoke to employees who say they trained AI before being let goDespite hundreds of billions of dollars being invested globally in AI, Quintos says there is still limited evidence about how much productivity many workplace tools actually deliver."There is a term called 'AI washing'," he says.Some layoffs are presented as being driven by AI when companies are in fact responding to weaker demand or slowing economic conditions, Quintos says.Attributing redundancies to AI, he adds, can make restructuring appear like technological progress rather than a response to market conditions.The next transitionLabour groups have told the BBC that existing employment laws in the Philippines govern redundancy but offer little guidance on how companies should introduce AI into workplaces or consult employees over its use.The Philippines' outsourcing sector is also non-unionised, leaving many workers with little formal say over how new technologies are deployed.The government says that it, and the private sector have a responsibility to retrain workers, and risks falling behind competitors like India and Singapore. "To be completely honest, I think we're slightly behind. We have to catch up," says Leandro Aguirre of the Philippines Department of Information and Communications Technology."We have to double our efforts to put our people in a position where they will not be displaced but actually thrive in this growing AI race."The government has committed to upskilling more than 300,000 outsourcing workers, but Aguirre acknowledges that the Philippines may need to rethink the economic model that helped make it an outsourcing centre."We relied heavily on foreign direct investment," he says. "But I think we also need to focus on local talent and local companies."The ambition, he says, is to build home-grown AI companies capable of creating higher-value jobs.Aguirre rejects calls for sweeping new AI legislation, arguing that existing labour, privacy and consumer protection laws can be adapted more quickly through regulatory guidance."The benefits of AI have to trickle down to people," he says. "It can't just benefit employers."For more than 20 years, the Philippines built one of the world's most successful outsourcing industries by selling the skills of its people to multinational companies.AI may not end that model, but it is certainly changing it, and risks leaving some workers behind.Additional reporting by Jaltson Akkanath Chummar and Regine Cabato

schema.headline: How AI is changing jobs in the Philippines' outsourcing industry

title: In Odesa, no-one is safe from Russia's new Black Sea strike campaign
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Russian missiles and drones are hammering Ukraine's Black Sea ports, like OdesaByPaul AdamsDiplomatic corresp
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Russian missiles and drones are hammering Ukraine's Black Sea ports, like OdesaByPaul AdamsDiplomatic correspondent in Odesa"My crane operator, my partner, died five metres from me… The driver remained in the cabin. He also died."Svitlana Halchenko winces as she remembers the Russian ballistic missile which exploded at work in Odesa, killing her colleagues. Svitlana works as a warehouse shift manager at the city's main port.Despite her injuries – she walks with a limp, pieces of shrapnel still embedded in her leg and back – Svitlana is determined to keep working.But her normally bustling workplace is largely silent.Russia is ramping up its efforts to strangle Ukraine's commercial links to the outside world, launching attacks all along the country's Black Sea coastline.From damaged port infrastructure to listing ships with bridges blackened and containers still smouldering, the evidence is everywhere. Nowhere more so than out towards the horizon, where the approaches to Ukraine's once bustling ports – Odesa, Chornomorsk, Pivdennyi – are almost devoid of ships.Svitlana maintains a brave smile throughout our conversation, but her distress is painfully obvious. Her fingers constantly twist a tissue as she tries to maintain her composure and she gazes into the distance as tears well up behind her glasses.The last few weeks have been worse than ever."It's been very difficult for morale," she says with a deep sigh. "A lot of sirens, a lot of shaheds [drones], a lot of hits. People are very tense."Maarten Lernout/BBCMy crane operator, my partner, died five metres from me… The driver remained in the cabin. He also diedAccording to Ukraine's port administration, July saw 57 Russian attacks on civilian vessels, 22 of them at sea, and a further 67 hits on port infrastructure.While there have been Russian attacks on international vessels before, they've never been so numerous or so deadly.On July 19, a Turkish-owned cargo vessel, Golden Leo, was struck by three Russian missiles, killing nine Indian and Syrian crew members and a Ukrainian pilot.The ship, carrying Ukrainian corn, sank off Odesa a week later.According to the global shipping journal Lloyd's List, the Black Sea may now be the most dangerous place for shipping in the world - with July the deadliest month for merchant seamen, external since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. At his union's offices in the port city, Oleg Grygoriuk, Chairman of the Marine Transport Workers Union of Ukraine, says his members are suffering."There are a lot of veterans who already served their country," he says, "and they literally say that being in the port is more scary than being on the front line."Odesa's proximity to Russian-occupied territory means that workers often have little time to react."A missile flies from Crimea within a minute," he says. "If you are sitting in a crane, you need three and a half minutes to get down and go to the shelter. There's literally no time to do that."On a rare visit to one of the area's main ports, we saw almost no sign of movement. Hundreds of metres of berths sat empty and towering gantry cranes stood idle as a skeleton crew conducted maintenance.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Odesa's port lies empty now as Russia steps up its attacksThe military authorities allowed the visit on strict condition that we neither name the facility nor film anything. Ukraine doesn't want Russia to know what has and hasn't been damaged or reveal details that might aid Moscow in further targeting.Two damaged cargo vessels were moored nearby. Both had suffered severe damage to the superstructure, where the bridge and crew quarters are located.Just one lone freighter was seen moving towards the port."My heart is broken," a senior manager told us on condition we didn't name him."Normally there's a queue, even out at sea, waiting for a berth.""There was a deal," he said, referring to the UN-brokered 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative, under which Russia agreed to lift its blockade on Ukraine's agricultural exports. The agreement established safe maritime corridors to Odesa's main ports."They stopped the deal in the middle of 2023, but they didn't start attacking it until recently," the manager said."Today they do it systematically."Halfway through our tour, sirens sounded, forcing us to seek shelter for several minutes as a Russian jet-powered drone flew overhead.Weary dock workers scanned their phones for updates until the all-clear sounded.The manager said recent alerts have forced the port to shut down for 15 out of 24 hours.Technically, the port is open, as are all the others in the area. There is no prohibition on commercial ships attempting to use them. But the risks are clearly too great for most shipowners."There is barely anybody who wants to call because there is a huge problem with people getting killed," says Andrey Stavnitser, co-owner and CEO of one of the largest ports in the area."We can see that the whole supply chain is on hold."Image caption, Russia has made Ukraine's Black Sea coastline incredibly dangerous for shippingStavnitser says Russia is almost certainly retaliating for Ukraine's recent, highly successful attacks on Russian shipping, including sanctioned vessels carrying oil, as well as other ships involved in ferrying supplies to Russian-occupied Crimea.Using its own drones, Ukraine's Operation MoLoChKa (which roughly translates as "Moscow will fall through Crimea") has struck around 200 Russian vessels, bringing traffic in the strategic Sea of Azov to a virtual standstill.Ukrainians bristle at the suggestion that Russia and Ukraine are playing the same game. Kyiv is attempting to loosen Moscow's grip on occupied territory, they point out, while Russia is preventing Ukraine from exporting badly needed grain to the international market.With Ukraine's summer grain harvest well under way, this is all happening at the worst possible time."It's the most sensitive period," says Volodymyr Slavinskyi, trading director for Nibulon, one of the country's leading grain exporters."Farmers need to quickly harvest grains from the fields, not to lose the crop. They need to be able to sell the crop they harvested and reinvest money in the next production cycle."The impact of a prolonged shutdown of Ukraine's ports are likely to be severe. Ukraine is one of the world's largest producers of grain and oilseeds, supplying around 6% of global wheat exports before Russia's full-scale invasion and 10% of corn exports. But reports suggest, external its export capacity has dropped by at least a third since Russia launched its full-scale invasion.The Black Sea remains a vital export route for the country. Last year, the Greater Odesa ports accounted for more than 73 million tonnes of Ukraine's maritime exports, with grain accounting for 38 million tonnes.With almost no vessels currently moving on Ukraine's Black Sea shipping corridor, traders are already counting the cost of this summer's closure."I would say we've already lost the ability to deliver to global customers around half a million or 700,000 metric tons of Ukrainian grains and oilseeds," Slavinskyi says.Image source, Kristina Volk/BBCImage caption, Volodymyr Slavinskyi says Ukraine has lost a huge amount of its export capacityAway from the port, Odesa is determined to show off a very different side. The summer season is in full swing. The beaches are packed as visitors descend on the Black Sea from all over Ukraine.Buskers perform on the city's famous Potemkin Stairs, while sunbathers barely flinch as the sirens sound and explosions rumble in the distance.In a video published on Monday, swimmers were seen removing a Russian drone from the water as holidaymakers look on.They know the risks. In late June, 26-year-old Daria Kravchenko was killed when shrapnel from an intercepted Russian drone landed on the beach.This week, holidaymakers on Russia's equally Black Sea coast suffered a similar fate when an intercepted Ukrainian drone crashed onto a busy beach.Local authorities said seven people were killed, including three children.It's not clear what Ukraine was targeting, but this war on ships and ports has many casual victims. Sailors, dockworkers or people simply unlucky enough to live or work nearby.Outside Odesa, after a recent drone explosion, we found 83-year-old Andrii Dudik, surveying the mangled wreckage of his house and garden.He was physically unscathed and remarkably sanguine about the drone that had shattered his routine afternoon nap just hours earlier."I was lying there, wondering what I was going to do this afternoon. Now I know," he joked.Did he feel like an accidental victim of Russia's attacks on the nearby ports, I asked him."Absolutely," he replied. "And I won't forget it."Additional reporting by Kristina Volk, Anastasiia Levchenko and Joshua Cheetham

schema.headline: In Odesa, no-one is safe from Russia's new Black Sea strike campaign

title: Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away
description: Image source, Phil Walter/Getty ImagesImage caption, The Afghan women's football team gathered for the first time since Fifa ruled they could represen
body: Image source, Phil Walter/Getty ImagesImage caption, The Afghan women's football team gathered for the first time since Fifa ruled they could represent their country in official matchesByMahjooba NowrouziBBC News Afghan LanguagesReporting fromAuckland, New ZealandThe changing room is busy with footballers going through their pre-match routines. Some stretch and tighten their boots, others embrace."Be strong as always because we are representing Afghan women," says midfielder Fatima Haidari to fellow members of Afghan Women United.Applause erupts in the room where an Afghan flag hangs and a patriotic song is played. As the women sing along some struggle to hold back tears.There's a final team huddle with words of encouragement from their coach before they head out to the pitch – a place that for years they had been told they did not belong.The 23-player squad, selected from Afghan players now living abroad, has travelled to New Zealand for a training camp and to play two unofficial friendly games against the Cook Islands.This is the first time they have been together since football governing body Fifa ruled in April that they could represent their country in official matches in the future.Image source, Afghan Women UnitedImage caption, The team hopes that in the future they will qualify for international competitions, such as the World Cup and the OlympicsPreviously, they would have needed the approval of the Afghanistan Football Federation. This was not possible under the Taliban, who returned to power in August 2021, imposing wide-ranging restrictions on women and girls, including barring them from secondary school and university, most professions and organised sport.The country's national women's team, formed in 2007, could no longer play and its members were among those evacuated and resettled in countries including Australia, the UK and Portugal.Years of campaigning led to the creation of a refugee team, which became Afghan Women United. Thanks to Fifa's ruling, it can now try to qualify for international competitions such as the Olympics and World Cup.Gathered in New Zealand, the squad is excited to be playing together - as asylum seekers living in various countries it has been hard for them to get the travel documents in order to train as a team over the past five years.Sitting in the hotel in Auckland the day before the match, Manozh Noori, who has short hair, wears a T-shirt and knee-length shorts - a look that she says has often drawn criticism from relatives for looking too masculine.As the 23-year-old speaks to BBC Global Women about her family, her voice begins to falter. She pauses, takes a deep breath and looks away for a moment before continuing. There are no tears, but the emotion is clear.Image caption, Manozh Noori buried her medals in her garden before she left AfghanistanNoori now lives in Australia but she grew up playing football with boys in the streets of Kabul.After seeing women's football on television, she secretly joined local clubs and gradually rose through the ranks in Afghanistan.She knew her older brother would disapprove so she tried to reduce the risk of being recognised by wearing a face covering.Over six years, she won league titles, national championships and individual awards.Eventually her success became impossible to hide. In about 2018 her fellow players persuaded her to remove her face covering for a TV interview, which was shown on the news along with highlights of their match.Then she had to face the reality that her brother might see it. "I was so scared," she recalls. "I kept thinking, 'He's going to see me. He's going to know.'"In desperation, she tried to stop the family from watching the news by turning off the electricity, but word soon reached her brother and he was furious, she says."He was screaming," Noori says. "'You told us you were studying. You said you wanted to become a teacher or a doctor. What is this?'"He threatened to cut his ties with the family if she didn't stop, she adds. "My mother was crying. She told me, 'He's the person who supports us financially. How are we going to survive?'"Image source, Manozh NooriImage caption, Noori (in blue) used to wear a face mask to hide her identity when playing in Afghanistan  Noori did stop playing for a while, but eventually started again. She says her other brother, who lives in Germany, sent money to help finance her dream.When the Taliban took over in 2021, Noori decided to flee, but first she buried her football medals and trophies in the garden of her family home.More than four years later, they remain there."One day I will go back and dig them out," she says, briefly smiling at the thought."Football helped me get my mum and sister out of Afghanistan," she says. Two years after she moved to Australia and established herself as a football player, she was able to bring them over as well.This meant her sister was able to study again - even though her brother didn't want them playing sports, he always supported their education.  "I hope my brother now realises I am not a bad person," says Noori.Afghan Reunited: The fight for footballBBC Global Women follows Afghan female footballers as they return to the pitchAs she and the team prepare for the matches in Auckland, many of them describe football as the reason they survived one of the most turbulent periods in their country's recent history."If I wasn't a footballer, I would still be in Afghanistan, one of millions of girls who are not allowed to study, speak up or choose their own future," says Mursal Sadat, who also lives in Australia.Now 24, she works as a football coach, youth facilitator and advocate for refugees, women's rights and human rights.Image caption, Mursal Sadat (kneeling right) was 19 when the Taliban returned to power - she was among those evacuated from Kabul in August 2021 In Afghanistan, she says she was often judged, harassed and told that no-one would want to marry a woman who played sport.Today she is engaged to a man who is still in Afghanistan, and says he and his family are supportive of her work and place on the national team. "They tell me, 'You are the pride of our family. We are so lucky to have you.'"As the players step out into the driving Auckland rain to face the Cook Islands, they channel their energy and determination, unfazed by the weather. They have faced much tougher conditions back home.As a teenager, defender Najma Arefi trained in temperatures above 45C (113F) because girls were often given the least desirable training slots.Still, she persisted.The 22-year-old's efforts eventually helped a Herat-based team win a national championship.The victory, she says, changed attitudes towards women's sport in the city."There were billboards of us across Herat," she recalls. "People were proud. More families started letting their daughters play football."She now lives in Doncaster in northern England. She arrived in the UK after the Taliban takeover.She describes herself as an extrovert and says she now has opportunities she never imagined growing up in Afghanistan.Image source, Phil Walter/Getty ImagesImage caption, Najma Arefi, pictured during one of the matches against the Cook Islands, moved to the UK after the Taliban returned to powerShe studies criminal justice at college, plays football and makes decisions independently. "Having that freedom is incredible," she says.Yet she admits she often feels guilty and desperately sad about the freedoms denied to women back home."Millions of girls don't have the chance to study or follow their dreams. I feel I have to make the most of every opportunity."Sometimes I put too much pressure on myself," she says, tears rolling down her face.She thanks Khalida Popal, who founded the original Afghan women's team, for pushing Fifa to recognise them now they are in exile.  "To receive Fifa's recognition without the approval of the Taliban" has made history, she says.This official status is "something I'll always be proud of", she says.When the BBC asked the Taliban's director for sports, Ahmadullah Wasiq, about Fifa backing the women's team, he declined to comment. But he said he would like Fifa to visit the country and resume its support for football there in general - the organisation largely withdrew after the Taliban came to power. Fifa has previously said any resumption of support would depend on women being allowed to play.The game in Auckland turns out to be unforgiving. A single goal in the first match hands the Cook Islands a 1-0 victory. Three days later, despite the Afghan team's best efforts, the Cook Islands win again, this time 3-0.Yet for the players, these matches represent something far more significant than two defeats.A return to the pitch and proof that despite exile, separation from their families and years of uncertainty, Afghanistan's women footballers refused to disappear.This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

schema.headline: Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away

title: Nirmal Purja: How a generation of record-setting guides died in a disaster which klled a climbing legend
description: Purja, 43, also known as Nims, was the leading figure of the 10-member international team up Broad Peak, the world's 12th highest mountain, when the a
body: Purja, 43, also known as Nims, was the leading figure of the 10-member international team up Broad Peak, the world's 12th highest mountain, when the avalanche struck."Nims of course was iconic and undisputedly amongst the best of his generation," says Ben Ayers, a longtime Everest reporter for Outside Magazine.Kili Pemba Sherpa and Pur Bahadur Gurung, who were also guiding the Broad Peak expedition, were "strong climbers with a solid resume", Ayers said.Kili Pemba, 46, had just earned the coveted mountaineering Grand Slam after completing his last of the 14 highest peaks, also known as eight-thousanders, in early July.Even before this crowning achievement, he was already among the best in the industry having been part of the Nepali team, led again by Purja, that completed the first winter ascent of K2 in January 2021.At the time, K2, the world's second highest peak, was the only one of the eight-thousanders not yet climbed in winter. But at 8,611m, K2 is known to be steeper, more unpredictable and deadlier than Everest (8,849m).Many have described Kili Pemba as humble and deeply committed in serving his clients. He'd led two double-leg amputees, on separate occasions, to the summits of Everest and Manaslu, the eighth-highest mountain."That was the toughest task for any guide, [Kili Pemba] did that with a lot of care," says Gyanendra Shrestha, a government official who was at Everest Base Camp during one of these climbs.Pur Bahadur Gurung, 37, scaled 12 of the 14 highest peaks and was one of only 100 Nepali guides certified by the International Federation of Mountain Guides Association (IFMGA)."It takes a lot of money, passion and dedication to become an IFMGA guide. This tells us a lot about Pur Bahadur's zeal for mountaineering," says Himal Gautam, a spokesman for Nepal's tourism department. "It also speaks to the unprecedented loss we have suffered on Broad Peak," he adds.In 2024, Pur Bahadur was part of the team that discovered a century-old boot on Everest, believed to be that of British climber Andrew Irvine, who vanished on the mountain in 1924.The other three Nepali guides who perished on Broad Peak last week include Gyaljen Sherpa, best known for scaling the third-highest mountain Kanchenjunga three times in one season – a feat that some colleagues say deserves a Guinness World Record.Then there's Nima Sherpa, 36, who scaled four eight-thousanders in 2026 alone, and Nawang Thindu Sherpa, who in his 20s was among Nepal's rising generation of mountain guides.Some credit Purja for bringing Pakistan onto the radar of mountaineers through his feat of scaling the 14 peaks in just over six months, which was documented in a Netflix film."Nims' success gave many [guides] and foreigners the courage to believe that this mountaineering crown was truly possible," says Iswari Paudel, acting president of the Nepal Mountaineering Association."This has made Pakistan a major overseas base for Nepali Sherpas. And while helping foreign climbers fulfil their dreams, many guides have themselves completed the 14 peaks," Iswari says.Ayers, the Everest reporter, says Purja helped "publicise a new era of mountaineering" which in many ways helped "democratise mountain-climbing", but also "fuelled commercialisation and risk".Because of how remote Pakistan's mountains are, it is far more challenging to organise expeditions there – a feat that only the best guides undertake, Sherpas tell the BBC."We have to fix our own ropes, cut our steps into the ice, and set up camps as we go along," says Nima Rinji Sherpa. The 20-year-old set a new record in 2024 as the youngest mountaineer to summit the world's 14 highest peaks."Even in an era of commercial mountaineering, we experience real, old-fashioned mountaineering [in Pakistan]," he says.But because the region is hard to access, climbers usually attempt two to three mountains per trip, which makes the itinerary very tight, Nima Rinji adds.In Nepal, by contrast, mountaineering infrastructure is well-developed. The main trekking routes towards Everest are lined with family-run lodges that offer beds, hot meals and other facilities.Emergency evacuations are also generally easier in the Himalayas, where there is an integrated network of rescue helicopters and aid outposts at high altitude, whereas the Karakoram range, being more isolated, features fewer accessible landing zones."In the Pakistan mountains, getting the helicopters to base camp already takes a lot more effort, let alone flying them above high camps. "Therefore, the Sherpas who are capable of working in high-pressure situations, and who have diverse experiences and multiple skills are the ones who will operate in Pakistan," Nima Rinji says.While the Broad Peak disaster may spur calls to tighten safety standards, many believe it will do little to change high-altitude tourism."Generally, these tragedies cause a moment of concern... but then things go back to how they were. It's difficult to say with any conviction that any accident in the mountains is 'preventable' as the inherent danger is so high... and that's part of the appeal," Ayers says.The mountaineering community is drawn to high-risk pursuits, says Medhavi Gulati, a researcher specialising in high-altitude mountaineering."Often, it's the dangers and risk of death that attracts people," she says.The existing generation of mountain guides will continue to crave the global fame and world records that their predecessors have attained, she says. "I don't think that appeal will ever go away," she says."We've seen disasters like this one before, and nothing changed," says expert mountaineer and writer Alan Arnette, who pointed to how an ice avalanche on Everest killed 16 Sherpas in April 2014, and the 11 climbers who died on K2 in 2008 after a massive chunk of ice broke off."I doubt the Broad Peak incident will have a significant impact, given history. I hope I'm wrong," he says.

schema.headline: Nirmal Purja: How a generation of record-setting guides died in a disaster which klled a climbing legend

title: Iranian footballers who defied Tehran become Australian citizens
description: Two Iranian female footballers who publicly defied their government have become Australian citizens.Atefeh Ramezanisadeh, 34, and Fatemeh Pasandideh,
body: Two Iranian female footballers who publicly defied their government have become Australian citizens.Atefeh Ramezanisadeh, 34, and Fatemeh Pasandideh, 22, were naturalised in Brisbane, Queensland, on Wednesday.Ramezanisadeh said it was a "truly special and unforgettable day", while her teammate said "this moment means more than words can express".They were among seven members of Iran's national team to be granted humanitarian visas while in Australia for the Women's Asian Cup in March - but the other five changed their minds and returned home.It was feared the team would face repercussions for refusing to sing the Iranian anthem at their opening match, just days after the US-Israeli war against Iran began.Under pressure from the Iranian community in Australia, authorities initially gave the players a chance to seek asylum – in the end though, only Ramezanisadeh and Pasandideh took up the offer. There was never any question about whether both would become citizens, but the decision comes as the Australian government prepares to introduce tougher visa rules aimed at cutting migration.The new rules are expected to include restricting the work and appeal rights of asylum seekers and a ban on visitors applying for family visas.The Australian government has come under increasing pressure from political opponents that promise stricter migration policy, while refugee groups have criticised Australia's current measures, saying they put the safety of asylum seekers at risk.Ramezanisadeh and Pasandideh were given their citizenship certificates at a ceremony attended by Australian Interior Minister Tony Burke."It's a new beginning and a place I'm proud to call home," Pasandideh said.Ramezanisadeh recalled "all the challenges we faced" and added that she felt "proud and deeply grateful to become an Australian citizen."The two players have since been training with A-League Women's team Brisbane Roar, planning to continue their elite sporting careers in Australia.The drama around the Iranian team unfolded against the background of the war back in their home country which began on 28 February, when Israel and the US launched joint air strikes.Concerns grew about the team's safety after footage emerged of a host on state TV calling them "traitors" who ought to be punished for their silence during the Iranian anthem on 2 March.Human rights activists have said the women who returned to Iran may have been pressured to reverse their decisions through threats against their families.Iran's sports ministry said at the time that the returnees had "defeated the enemy's plans" against them through their "national spirit and patriotism".

schema.headline: Iranian footballers who defied Tehran become Australian citizens

title: Drone carrying explosives found at Leipzig airport in Germany
description: A drone carrying an explosive device has been found at a German airport, police say.A robot was deployed at Leipzig/Halle Airport after the device was
body: A drone carrying an explosive device has been found at a German airport, police say.A robot was deployed at Leipzig/Halle Airport after the device was spotted by an employee near Ukrainian cargo planes overnight, according to Saxony police. A second unidentified object also collided with a cargo aircraft near the same airport. It landed in Hanover with minor damage.Germany's interior minister said the incidents showed a "new level of threat". German airports are on high alert following several unauthorised drone flights in recent months over military bases, airports, energy terminals, seaports and logistics companies. Police have warned of a potential Russian involvement which Moscow has denied. Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany is used by the Germany military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carry most of the country's aerial cargo.It is also a major hub for the logistics group, DHL.A police spokesman told the BBC that the explosive-laden object had been spotted close to parked Antonov planes.The detonator was removed from the explosive device. Police later carried out a controlled explosion. Flights on the northern runway resumed at 01:55 (23:55 GMT on Tuesday). The southern runway remains closed."All of this does not point to an amateurish approach. We are talking about a professional, hybrid threat scenario that we will continue to address," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said.He did not name any suspects, but suggested the investigation may point to a possible "competition" that "may also involve foreign powers". Ukraine's Ambassador to Germany Oleksii Makeiev told Welt TV: "Who else could it be but Russia?"Russia has not commented.Similar incidents with suspicious drones in Germany have only happened since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Peter R Neumann, a professor of Security Studies at King's College London, said on X."Since last night, the drone war has reached Germany. And it exposes a weakness that we've known about for years," he said.In July 2024 a parcel burst into flames on the ground at Leipzig/Halle Airport before it could be loaded onto a DHL cargo plane, one of a series of parcel fires that targeted the UK and EU countries. There are suspicions it could have been sabotage linked to Moscow.The parcels had contained explosive devices that were set off by electronic timers hidden in vibrating massage pillows, according to authorities.Russia has denied any involvement in those incidents.Last year a Chinese woman was convicted  for passing on information about flight schedules and cargo movements at Leipzig/Halle Airport to a man spying for Beijing.

schema.headline: Drone carrying explosives found at Leipzig airport in Germany
